Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be on guard all the time

vignette: Lina, a 22-year-old South Eastern Asian woman, has been married for just over a year and works as a call center agent in a bustling office. Her life took an unexpected turn when she was sexually assaulted on her way home from work one evening. The assault left her feeling profoundly violated and unsafe. Since the incident, Lina has experienced intense triggers that are tied to specific contexts and emotions. Ambulances passing by her house or loud sirens at night remind her of the chaos and fear she felt during the assault. Stressful situations, such as arguments with her husband or deadlines at work, can trigger vivid flashbacks that make her feel like she is reliving the event. Even seeing happy families on TV or in public has become a painful reminder of what she lost-her sense of safety and normalcy. These triggers have led Lina to adopt several maladaptive strategies to cope with the overwhelming distress they cause. She avoids any reminders of the assault, such as conversations about similar incidents, and tries to manage her tension through sexual fantasies or activities that provide temporary relief but do not address the underlying trauma. Additionally, she steers clear of authority figures like police officers in uniform, believing they might only bring back painful memories. The vividness and fragmented nature of her memory exacerbate these struggles. When Lina thinks about the assault, her recollections feel more real than any ordinary memory, often accompanied by a distinct taste that she associates with that night. These fragmented pieces of memory are jumbled and disconnected, making it difficult for her to form a coherent narrative of what happened. Lina's negative appraisals further complicate her situation. She believes that if she thinks about the assault too much, she will not be able to handle the emotional weight of it all. This thought-avoidance has led to hypervigilance; Lina feels like she must constantly be on guard, scanning for exits and signs of danger in every new environment. Her sense of inadequacy intensifies her distress, as she believes that she cannot manage or recover from this trauma. The interplay between these components creates a self-reinforcing cycle. When she encounters triggers such as ambulances or stress at work, Lina's memory is instantly flooded with vivid fragments and sensory details of the assault, making her feel like she is back in danger. This leads her to engage in maladaptive strategies, avoiding reminders and focusing on sexual fantasies to cope. Her negative appraisals also drive her to avoid situations that might trigger these memories further. The belief that she cannot handle thinking about the event makes her hyper-vigilant, constantly scanning for exits and signs of danger as a way to protect herself from potential threats. This hypervigilance reinforces her sense of inadequacy, making her feel like she is forever marked by this trauma. In her daily life, Lina's avoidance behaviors have had concrete consequences. Her work performance has suffered because the stressors at her call center job trigger her distress, and she often finds herself withdrawing from conversations with colleagues for fear they might mention something that reminds her of the assault. This withdrawal has strained her relationships, particularly with her husband, who notices that she is increasingly distant. The final straw came when Lina found herself overwhelmed by a combination of triggers at work-stressful deadlines, an authority figure in uniform visiting the office, and a colleague's story about a similar incident. She realized then that her coping mechanisms were no longer sufficient to manage the intensity of her symptoms. What frightened her most was not only her inability to control these reactions but also her growing sense that she might never regain a semblance of normalcy. Seeking help became Lina's last hope for reclaiming some measure of peace and safety in her life. She is most afraid of continuing to feel trapped by the trauma, yet she remains hopeful that with support, she can learn to navigate and manage her distress without being consumed by it.
